newsitem.title: CHINA: Constitutional uncertainty dogs China-ruled HK.
newsitem.headline: Constitutional uncertainty dogs China-ruled HK.

text.p: A Hong Kong court is likely to avoid making a clear-cut ruling on a landmark case challenging the territory's post-colonial constitutional and legal systems, political and legal experts said on Friday.

The agonising over a potential constitutional crisis could be prolonged as Hong Kong's appeals court was not likely to deliver any verdict on the unelected Provisional Legislature, whose legality was called into question via a conspiracy case.

They said the judgment expected next Tuesday would probably focus on the status of the criminal case, allowing the three judges to avoid ruling on the status of the chamber, a complex issue with far-reaching consequences.

"I don't think it is very likely that the court of appeal will hand down a definitive ruling on the legality of the Provisional Legislature. It is simply not necessary for them to do so, in this particular case," one lawyer said.
"The judges may or may not rule on the legality of the Provisional Legislature," another legal expert said.

Their comments follow a three-day court hearing which saw three prominent lawyers pitted against the government over the status of the chamber, a case which grew from a criminal trial into a constitutional conundrum.

Lawyers argued the defendants should be set free because laws under which they were charged ceased to be valid when the chamber failed to formally adopt them after Britain's handover of Hong Kong to China on July 1, leaving a legal vacuum.
The argument throws into doubt the status and legality of the China-backed legislature, installed after the handover to replace an elected assembly.

The challenge also strikes at the heart of the legal system and Hong Kong institutions, as the chamber has endorsed the appointment of senior judges and passed crucial laws governing migrants and labour laws since it was sworn in.

Leading the attack was former Bar chairwoman Gladys Li, who argued the chamber did not find any basis in the Basic Law, Hong Kong's post-handover constitution, and flouted rules for the first post-colonial assembly set by China's parliament.

Solicitor General Daniel Fung, representing the government, said the chamber, cobbled together by a China-appointed body and endorsed by China's parliament, was a legal necessity given the end of British sovereignty and the start of Chinese rule.

Hong Kong courts had no right to rule on the chamber as it was a creation of China's parliament, Fung said, warning that nullifying the body would be invalid as the judges themselves owed their jobs to the chamber.
But analysts said the appeals court could sidestep the issue of the chamber's status as it was not central to the criminal case.

"The court does not need to come to a view on the legality of the Provisional Legislature before they can rule on that other issue -- whether the common law offence of conspiracy survives the handover," the lawyer said.
But he rejected suggestions that judges may avoid ruling on the body out of fear.
"I don't think our judges will behave so evasively. Our judges won't be afraid," he said.
The experts said the question of the Provisional Legislature's legality must be addressed sooner or later.
"If they delay to decide that matter, it can create quite a degree of uncertainty and confusion," said law professor Nihal Jayawickrama.
